intro.title: Cacao & Empire
intro.subtitle: France, Martinique, and their role in the creation of a globalized economy

stops.title: Saint-Pierre

narrative: Saint-Pierre was the main port of Martinique, an early major hub of Cacao production and exportation. Originally used for sugar and cotton production, the first Cacao trees were not planted on Martinique until 1660. The island was originally under the control of Pierre Bélain, sieur (lord) d’Esnambuc before later being passed down to his nephew Jacques-Dyel du Parquet who purchased the island from him. It was then placed under the control of the West Indies Company in 1664. Then in 1673, the French crown took control of the island under the Pacte Colonial, a policy in which all exports had to first go through France as a way to grow the mainland’s economy. Martinique relied heavily on enslaved labor to support the production of Cacao. In 1727 an earthquake struck the island devastating its crops and forcing a temporary halt in production. The island did not pick back up large scale production until 1740 when hardier plant breeds were imported and demand picked up.

firsthand.quote: “From this battery as far as that of Saint Robert, which is at the far end on the western side, is the quarter that is called the Mouillage, because all the ships anchor in front of that place; the anchorage there is excellent, and the ships are much better sheltered there and much safer than in front of Fort Saint Pierre.”
firsthand.importance: Labat’s description of the Mouillage, where “all the ships anchor,” helps explain why Saint-Pierre became the commercial center of the colony: an export crop like cacao, which Labat priced for sale in France, depended on safe access to shipping.

stops.globalization: Martinique shows how the French Empire used different parts of the world and their climates as a way to grow and export certain goods. The desire for a European country to mass produce a South American crop was a driving force behind the creation of a globalized economy. The use of an island colony such as Martinique demonstrates the importance of globalization through the utilization of African labor, American soil, and European infrastructure.

sources.citation: Jean-Baptiste Labat, Nouveau voyage aux isles de l’Amérique, vol. 1 (Paris: Giffart, 1722)

stops.title: Nantes

scene.alt: Painted illustration of the Quai de la Fosse in Nantes on the river Loire: a three-masted French ship lies at the quay with sailors in its rigging while a wooden crane swings a net of cargo aboard. On the cobbled quay, workers carry rolls of brightly printed cotton cloth, roll barrels, carry a small chest and handle coiled rope, and a cooper hammers a hoop onto a cask. In the centre a shipowner in a powdered wig and the ship's captain in a blue coat and tricorne talk while a clerk notes the cargo in a ledger. Along the left stand the tall pale stone houses of the shipowners, with a horse and cart before them, and small boats cross the river toward the far bank.

narrative: Nantes, France was the main port in France where ships departed from to head out towards Western Africa to engage in the Atlantic Slave Trade. An enslaved person's life expectancy working on a French colony was around twenty years, as a result many trips to West Africa were made in order to keep up with the necessary labor to meet growing demands. Ships would leave the port with goods such as gunpowder, weapons, textiles, utensils, and tobacco, which would then be traded with African rulers and merchants in exchange for slaves.
stops.globalization: This port allowed France to prepare and send out ships that would acquire the forced labor they used to fuel the globalization of goods. This was their main connection point to Africa and the starting point for their system of global trade and exploitation.

sources.citation: Château des ducs de Bretagne, "Nantes and the Atlantic Slave Trade," Google Arts & Culture

scene.alt: Painted illustration of the French trading post on Gorée Island: on the beach a woman pounds millet in a tall wooden mortar while another sifts grain in a basket; African porters carry bales and goods to a painted pirogue drawn up on the sand; at a table under a fringed parasol a French clerk in a tricorne hat writes in a ledger beside an African trader in white robes. Along the shore a line of captive Africans is led under guard toward the boats. Pirogues rowed by African oarsmen cross the bay to a three-masted French ship at anchor, below a stone fort flying the white fleur-de-lis flag, with a baobab tree and colonial stone houses with wooden balconies on the right.

narrative: West Africa was the primary destination for ships leaving Nantes and other local French ports. The ships would use the goods they brought to trade in exchange for enslaved people who were captured in wars and raids between African states. It could take a French slave ship three to six months on the coast of West Africa going to different trading posts before they could fill up their ships with enslaved people.
stops.globalization: West Africa shows how globalization was more than just the transfer of goods between countries and was also the forced removal and relocation of people in order to exploit their labor. As demand for labor increased so did warfare between African nations as a way to capture more people to be traded for goods with the Europeans. Enslaved labor was a large factor that allowed for globalization to occur as rapidly as it did.

sources.citation: Château des ducs de Bretagne, "Nantes and the Atlantic Slave Trade," Google Arts & Culture

narrative: The port of Bayonne, located in the South-West of France near Spain, became a regional hub for the reception of raw cacao, its production into chocolate, and later its exportation throughout France and other parts of Europe. It marked the point at which cacao, acquired through a globalized system of trade, arrived and was to be distributed throughout France. A community of Sepharic Jews who were exiled from Spain fled to this area of France. They played a key role in the production of chocolate goods and their spread across Europe.
stops.globalization: Bayonne shows how the importation of foreign goods influenced local knowledge and created new trades and jobs otherwise not available. As cacao importations and its popularity increased, so did the availability of knowledge around how to process and distribute it, brought by knowledgeable migrants. This opened up new jobs such as chocolatiers that had not previously existed.

sources.citation: On the Chocolate Trail, "That time Jews smuggled chocolate to France (and a recipe for Basque chocolate cake)" (July 2016)

stops.title: Versailles

A lady with a fan sits on a sofa beside a small spaniel on a cushion, and two gentlemen sip chocolate at tall open windows overlooking the formal gardens and the Grand Canal, under a crystal chandelier.

narrative: After the Royal Court moved to Versailles in 1682 it quickly became the center of demand for cacao. King Louis XIV and his wife were known to enjoy the product. He had previously granted David Chaillou a royal monopoly and the sole privilege of manufacturing and selling chocolate in 1652. Through mercantilism, the French crown was able to remain in control of the trade of a good that was only consumed by elites, showing the power that a small group of individuals held over a globalized economy.
stops.globalization: The demand, however, was first only from the wealthy, meaning the cost of growing, harvesting, and then shipping cacao was difficult to profit from. The trade was made worthwhile by the fact that French planters in Martinique relied on enslaved people from Africa. In the late 1600s, the majority of the people on the island were enslaved people, keeping the cost of producing Cacao low and allowing planters and merchants to profit. King Louis XIV reinforced this system by signing the Code Noir in 1685, a law that defined enslaved peoples within the French colonies as property and gave royal approval to the plantation owners in the colonies. In this way, the hot chocolate enjoyment of the nobility depended on the backs of enslaved people suffering in Martinique.

sources.citation: Château de Versailles, "Hot chocolate at Versailles" (Key dates)
